books.title: Two Boys Kissing
books.author: David Levithan
books.ratingNote: Consistently high reader ratings with strong emotional response.
reviewSummary: Told through a Greek-chorus-style narration of gay men lost to AIDS, the novel follows two boys attempting to break the record for the longest kiss. Readers frequently describe the book as both celebratory and mournful, praising how it connects queer history with present-day love and visibility. Many reviews highlight the emotional weight of the narration, noting that it transforms a simple act into a statement about survival, memory, and joy. The book is often described as short but profoundly affecting.

books.title: Take Me with You When You Go
books.author: David Levithan & Jennifer Niven
books.ratingNote: Strong ratings driven by emotional reader engagement.
reviewSummary: Structured around unanswered questions after a teen girl disappears, the novel explores grief, love, and the stories people leave behind. Readers praise the fragmented, poetic format, noting how it mirrors the confusion of loss and longing. Reviews often emphasize that the book focuses less on mystery-solving and more on emotional aftermath. Many describe it as haunting and quietly devastating.

books.title: Someday
books.author: David Levithan
books.ratingNote: Steady ratings from readers familiar with the Every Day universe.
reviewSummary: Returning to the world of Every Day, this novel explores love from a different perspective, focusing on longing, autonomy, and emotional imbalance. Readers often note the more introspective tone, appreciating the way it complicates ideas of destiny and romance. Reviews highlight that the book asks uncomfortable questions about desire and consent rather than offering easy answers. It resonates most with readers who enjoy reflective storytelling.

books.title: Another Day
books.author: David Levithan
books.ratingNote: Consistent reader engagement within the companion-novel format.
reviewSummary: This companion to Every Day retells the story through Rhiannon’s eyes, offering a more grounded and conflicted emotional arc. Readers frequently mention that the shift in perspective adds realism and moral tension to the story. Reviews praise the exploration of boundaries and self-worth within relationships. Many say it deepens the original narrative rather than repeating it.

books.title: The Mysterious Disappearance of Aidan S.
books.author: David Levithan
books.ratingNote: Positive reception for its quiet, character-driven approach.
reviewSummary: After a teen vanishes and then inexplicably returns, the story focuses on the emotional ripple effects rather than the mystery itself. Readers appreciate the understated tone and the way relationships shift in response to absence. Reviews often highlight how the book captures the discomfort of not having clear answers. It is described as subtle and thoughtful rather than suspense-driven.

books.title: Every Day
books.author: David Levithan
books.ratingNote: Long-standing popularity with a wide YA readership.
reviewSummary: Following a person who wakes up in a different body each day, the novel explores identity, love, and empathy. Readers praise the high-concept premise and its emotional implications, especially how it challenges assumptions about gender and selfhood. Reviews often mention that the romance is both tender and frustrating. It remains widely discussed for its ideas as much as its story.

books.title: Boy Meets Boy
books.author: David Levithan
books.ratingNote: Beloved by readers seeking joyful queer stories.
reviewSummary: Set in a deliberately accepting town, the novel presents a rom-com-style queer love story centered on joy rather than trauma. Readers appreciate the hopeful, idealized setting and playful tone. Reviews often describe it as comforting and affirming, especially for younger readers. It is frequently recommended as an entry point into LGBTQ+ YA.

books.title: The Upside of Unrequited
books.author: Becky Albertalli
books.ratingNote: Consistently positive reception from contemporary romance readers.
reviewSummary: The novel follows Molly, a fat, anxious teen navigating friendships and first love while dealing with chronic crushes. Readers praise the body-positive representation and the focus on internal growth rather than dramatic plot twists. Reviews often highlight the warmth of the family dynamics and queer representation. Many describe it as comforting and relatable.

books.title: What If It’s Us
books.author: Becky Albertalli & Adam Silvera
books.ratingNote: Large reader base with stable ratings.
reviewSummary: A chance meeting in New York sparks a queer rom-com about fate, timing, and missed connections. Readers enjoy the witty dialogue and city setting, often praising the authenticity of the teen voices. Reviews frequently mention the realistic, open-ended conclusion. It is popular with readers who like romance that allows for ambiguity.

books.title: Here’s to Us
books.author: Becky Albertalli & Adam Silvera
books.ratingNote: Positive reception among fans of the first book.
reviewSummary: This sequel revisits Arthur and Ben as they reconsider their relationship after time apart. Readers praise the emotional honesty around jealousy, growth, and second chances. Reviews often note that it works best for readers invested in the original pairing. The tone is more reflective than the first book.

books.title: We’ll Fly Away
books.author: Bryan Bliss
books.ratingNote: Strong emotional response from readers, with ratings clustering around 4 stars.
reviewSummary: Told partly through letters written from death row, the novel traces a friendship shaped by poverty, abuse, and impossible choices. Readers frequently describe the book as heartbreaking but compassionate, praising its refusal to simplify blame or morality. Reviews often highlight how the structure builds dread slowly rather than relying on shock. Many readers say it leaves them thinking long after finishing.

books.title: All My Rage
books.author: Sabaa Tahir
books.ratingNote: Extremely high reader ratings across platforms.
reviewSummary: The novel interweaves the lives of Pakistani American teens Noor and Salahudin with flashbacks to Salahudin’s mother, exploring family loyalty, addiction, and generational trauma. Readers overwhelmingly describe the book as devastating yet cathartic, praising its emotional honesty and depth. Reviews frequently note how the characters’ mistakes feel painfully real rather than dramatic. Many readers consider it one of the most emotionally powerful YA novels they’ve read.
books.ageNote: 15+; domestic violence, substance abuse, and trauma.

books.title: Love from A to Z
books.author: S.K. Ali
books.ratingNote: Consistently high ratings, especially from readers seeking Muslim representation.
reviewSummary: Structured through alternating journal entries, the story follows two Muslim teens who meet while traveling and gradually open up about faith, illness, and grief. Readers praise the warmth and sincerity of the romance, noting that vulnerability is treated as strength rather than weakness. Reviews often highlight the thoughtful portrayal of chronic illness and doubt. Many describe the book as comforting while still emotionally grounded.

books.title: Queen of the Tiles
books.author: Hanna Alkaf
books.ratingNote: Strong ratings among readers who enjoy quieter mysteries.
reviewSummary: Set at a Malaysian Scrabble tournament, the novel blends mystery with grief as a teen receives messages from her deceased friend’s social media account. Readers praise the atmosphere and cultural specificity, noting that the puzzle unfolds slowly and emotionally. Reviews often mention the focus on friendship and burnout rather than action. The story is described as thoughtful and unsettling rather than suspense-heavy.

books.title: The Weight of the Stars
books.author: K. Ancrum
books.ratingNote: Strong reader enthusiasm despite niche appeal.
reviewSummary: A quiet, character-driven story about found family and queer love, framed by the looming distance of space travel. Readers frequently praise the tenderness of the relationships and the butch lesbian protagonist. Reviews highlight the slow pacing as a strength, allowing emotional bonds to feel earned. Many describe the book as gentle but deeply affecting.

books.title: Other Side of the Tracks
books.author: Charity Alyse
books.ratingNote: Positive reception from readers seeking socially conscious YA.
reviewSummary: Told from multiple perspectives in two racially divided towns, the novel examines how violence and segregation shape teen relationships. Readers often describe the book as intense and uncomfortable, praising its willingness to sit with moral ambiguity. Reviews highlight the layered characterization and community dynamics. It is frequently compared to other big-issue YA novels.

books.title: Even If It Breaks Your Heart
books.author: Erin Hahn
books.ratingNote: Generally strong reader ratings.
reviewSummary: Two teens bond through country music while dealing with family pressure and small-town expectations. Readers praise the emotional honesty and music-centered storytelling. Reviews often highlight the balance between romance and self-discovery. The tone is described as heartfelt without being overly sentimental.

books.title: Nothing Ever Happens Here
books.author: Sarah Hagger-Holt
books.ratingNote: Steady reader response with strong emotional engagement.
reviewSummary: A teen copes with her father’s gender transition while navigating secrecy and fear at school. Readers frequently praise the compassionate portrayal of family change and trans identity. Reviews note that the story focuses on love and adjustment rather than conflict alone. It is often described as quiet but impactful.

books.title: Thirst
books.author: Varsha Bajaj
books.ratingNote: Positive reception for its focused, urgent narrative.
reviewSummary: Set in India, the novel follows a girl fighting to secure water for her family during a severe drought. Readers praise the tight pacing and sense of urgency. Reviews often highlight how environmental crisis is personalized through one family’s struggle. The story is described as intense and educational without being preachy.

books.title: We Deserve Monuments
books.author: Jas Hammonds
books.ratingNote: Strong emotional response from readers.
reviewSummary: A multigenerational story exploring racism, grief, and buried family truths in a Southern town. Readers praise the lyrical prose and layered timelines. Reviews frequently note the emotional payoff as histories intersect. Many describe the book as heavy but rewarding.

books.title: Ahmed Aziz’s Epic Year
books.author: Nina Hamza
books.ratingNote: Generally positive reception among younger YA readers.
reviewSummary: A lighthearted story following a Muslim teen navigating school, friendships, and family expectations. Readers enjoy the humor and relatability of the protagonist. Reviews often mention that the tone stays upbeat while still addressing cultural identity. It is frequently recommended for middle-to-early high school readers.

books.title: Even If It Breaks Your Heart
books.author: Erin Hahn
books.ratingNote: Consistent ratings across platforms.
reviewSummary: Set against a backdrop of country music competitions, the novel explores ambition, love, and self-doubt. Readers praise the emotional realism and music-infused atmosphere. Reviews highlight how the characters’ growth feels earned rather than idealized. The romance is described as sincere and grounded.

books.title: Songs of Irie
books.author: Asha Bromfield
books.ratingNote: Steady appreciation from readers seeking historical context.
reviewSummary: Set in 1970s Jamaica, the novel weaves music, class difference, and political unrest into a coming-of-age story. Readers praise the vivid sense of place and atmosphere. Reviews often note the slower pacing but strong emotional immersion. It appeals to readers interested in history-inflected contemporary fiction.

books.title: Georgia Peaches and Other Forbidden Fruit
books.author: Jaye Robin Brown
books.ratingNote: Solid reception within queer YA readership.
reviewSummary: A queer rom-com set in a conservative town, exploring faith, family, and authenticity. Readers appreciate the nuanced portrayal of religious characters. Reviews highlight the kindness and humor of the romance. The book is often described as both frustrating and affirming by design.

books.title: Only Mostly Devastated
books.author: Sophie Gonzales
books.ratingNote: Consistent popularity among romance readers.
reviewSummary: A Grease-inspired queer romance about a summer fling complicated by closeting and peer pressure. Readers praise the humor and strong friend group dynamics. Reviews often mention the emotional realism of internalized homophobia. The tone balances fun with genuine hurt.

books.title: Flip the Bird
books.author: Kym Brunner
books.ratingNote: Niche but positive reader response.
reviewSummary: A contemporary story centered on falconry, family tension, and first love. Readers enjoy the unique subject matter and grounded romance. Reviews often describe the mystery elements as light but engaging. The book appeals to readers looking for something different.

books.title: Admission
books.author: Julie Buxbaum
books.ratingNote: Moderate ratings with strong discussion potential.
reviewSummary: A teen confronts privilege and complicity after learning her parents bribed her way into college. Readers praise the moral discomfort and refusal to offer easy redemption. Reviews often note that the protagonist is intentionally hard to like at first. The book sparks conversation about accountability.

books.title: Sasha Masha
books.author: Agnes Borinsky
books.ratingNote: Deeply appreciated by a smaller subset of readers.
reviewSummary: A quiet, introspective novel about gender questioning and drifting into queer community spaces. Readers who connect with the book describe it as dreamy and emotionally honest. Reviews often emphasize its ambiguity as a strength rather than a flaw. Best suited for readers comfortable with open-ended narratives.

books.title: Kings, Queens, and In-Betweens
books.author: Tanya Boteju
books.ratingNote: Strong niche enthusiasm.
reviewSummary: A joyful exploration of drag culture and queer community as a shy teen finds belonging. Readers praise the celebratory tone and focus on chosen family. Reviews often mention that joy, rather than trauma, drives the story. The book is described as affirming and fun.
